lesson.title: Clock & Numbers Gym
lesson.subtitle: tien, twintig, honderd, duizend — and the half-hour trap

hook.title: Numbers First, Clock Second
hook.content: Tien, twintig, honderd, duizend: the number spine is almost English. Once the numbers are secure, the clock becomes a small reading rule instead of a second vocabulary list.

pattern.title: Name the number, then the hour
pattern.content: Tien uur, half vier, honderd euro, duizend boeken. The number comes first; uur marks the clock. Half vier is 3:30 because Dutch is counting toward four.
pattern.trap_note: Do not translate half vier as 4:30. The half-hour is named for the hour it is approaching.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Clock & Numbers Gym):
exercises.target_answer: tien, twintig, honderd, duizend, half, het uur
exercises.meaning: ten, twenty, hundred, thousand, half, hour
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Clock & Numbers Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “It is half past three.”?
exercises.explanation: “Het is half vier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Clock & Numbers Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Name the number, then the hour
It means: I have a hundred euros.
exercises.explanation: “Ik heb honderd euro.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Name the number, then the hour.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not translate half vier as 4:30. The half-hour is named for the hour it is approaching.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Duizend is veel.” is word-for-word “A thousand is much.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Name the number, then the hour.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: It is ten o'clock.
exercises.explanation: “Het is tien uur.” reuses only material taught in “Clock & Numbers Gym” — Name the number, then the hour.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het is tien uur.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Name the number, then the hour.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “We come at three o'clock.”
twist.explanation: Om marks clock time; the number and uur stay together.

summary.outcome: Use Dutch numbers up to a thousand and read the clock without translating half literally.
summary.takeaway: The clock is a rule, not a list: learn the anchor and the rest follows.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Days, Months & Dates.

tien.etymology_derivation: English ten and Dutch tien are the same word.

twintig.etymology_derivation: English twenty and Dutch twintig are the same word; age uses zijn.

honderd.etymology_derivation: The same word as English hundred.

duizend.etymology_derivation: English thousand and Dutch duizend are the same word.

half.etymology_derivation: Dutch half counts toward the next hour: half drie = 2:30.

uur.etymology_derivation: Latin hōra gave English hour and Dutch uur.
